articles.title: Webb reveals stunning panorama of star formation
articles.description: This starry view of the nearby star-forming region IC 348 is one of the largest images from the NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope released to the public so far. Using Webb, astronomers searched IC 348 for brown dwarfs, which are less massive than the smallest stars. The researchers discovered brown dwarfs just twice the mass of Jupiter, bringing the study of these curious objects into a new mass range.
articles.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope reveals a spectacular panoramic view of star formation in the nearby IC 348 region. This landmark observation showcases the power of JWST to image stellar nurseries in extraordinary detail.

articles.title: Astronomers Directly Image the Youngest Exoplanet Ever
articles.description: Most exoplanets we find have been around a long time. They’ve cleared out their orbital path (one of the requirements of planethood, as fans of Pluto well know), have their own gravitational pull, and in many cases shine with their own infrared light. But it takes a long time to get to that point - finding “young” planets is much harder. But a new paper available in The Astrophysical Journal Letters by a research team led by Andrea Bernardi of Diego Portales University in Chile describes a new paper that definitely takes the prize as the youngest exoplanet we’ve yet found.
articles.summary: Astronomers directly imaged the youngest known exoplanet, providing unprecedented insights into planetary formation and early development. This landmark discovery opens new windows into understanding how planetary systems are born.

articles.title: NASA's Hubble seeks lensed supernova, marks 200,000 orbits
articles.description: NASA's Hubble Space Telescope completed its 200,000th orbit around Earth on Sept. 19, marking another milestone for an observatory that continues to transform our understanding of the universe.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: NASA's Hubble Space Telescope achieved its 200,000th orbit while continuing to discover lensed supernovae. This landmark celebrates decades of groundbreaking contributions to astronomy.

articles.title: NASA just powered up Roman’s massive 300-megapixel camera
articles.description: NASA’s Roman Space Telescope has successfully activated its 300-megapixel infrared camera, which will capture enormous stretches of the cosmos with Hubble-like sharpness. Its planet-hunting coronagraph is also working as expected, putting Roman another major step closer to beginning science operations in 2027.
articles.summary: NASA's Roman Space Telescope successfully activated its revolutionary 300-megapixel infrared camera. This milestone promises unprecedented views of the universe across vast cosmic distances.

articles.title: Astronomers Confirm Youngest Known Planet, Less Than 1 Million Years Old
articles.description: Astronomers have confirmed the youngest known planet yet, a Jupiter-size world less than 1 million years old that orbits a star about 450 light-years from Earth, according to a study published Sept. 16 in The Astrophysical Journal Letters. The planet, designa…
articles.summary: Astronomers have confirmed the youngest known planet ever discovered, a Jupiter-sized world less than 1 million years old still in its formation stage. This landmark finding provides unprecedented insights into planetary birth and early development.

articles.title: Новая статья: Шпионское наследство и триумф баллистики: как телескоп „Нэнси Грейс Роман“ отправился переписывать космологию
articles.description: 30 августа 2026 года со стартового комплекса LC-39A во Флориде была запущена новейшая флагманская обсерватория NASA — Космический телескоп имени Нэнси Грейс Роман NGRST (Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope). Аппарат, чей путь от чертежей до стартового стола зан…
articles.summary: NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope launched on August 30, 2026, becoming the agency's newest flagship observatory poised to transform cosmology. This mission represents a major milestone in space-based astronomy and our ability to study the universe.

articles.title: Juice to fly past Earth for third gravity assist
articles.description: The European Space Agency’s Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer (Juice) will return to Earth on 28 September, with flight controllers guiding the spacecraft close to our home planet to alter its speed and direction en route to Jupiter.
articles.summary: The European Space Agency's JUICE spacecraft will perform its third Earth gravity assist on September 28, continuing its journey toward Jupiter and its icy moons. This critical maneuver helps position the spacecraft for its mission to explore potentially habitable ocean worlds.

articles.title: BepiColombo begins Mercury arrival with MTM separation success
articles.description: On 3 September 2026 at 15:49 CEST, the European Space Agency's BepiColombo Mission Control Team at the European Space Operations Centre (ESOC) received the signal they had been waiting for – BepiColombo’s Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) successfully separated from the spacecraft stack. This landmark achievement for the ESA and Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) mission marks the first step of BepiColombo's long-awaited arrival at Mercury.
articles.summary: BepiColombo successfully completed its Mercury transfer module separation on September 3, 2026, marking the beginning of its Mercury arrival sequence. This milestone represents a critical phase in the ESA/JAXA mission to study the solar system's innermost planet.

articles.title: BepiColombo’s Mercury arrival begins - full replay
articles.description:
Video: 
			02:31:10
				
Watch the replay of the livestream originally broadcast on 3 September as ESA/JAXA's BepiColombo mission took the first critical step towards arriving at Mercury.
After travelling through the inner Solar System together for eight years, BepiColombo's Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) will separate from the rest of the stacked spacecraft on 3 September 2026. This marks the beginning of one of the most complex planetary arrival sequences ever attempted by ESA.
Broadcast live from ESA's European Space Operations Centre (ESOC) in Darmstadt, Germany, the programme includes live views from the iconic Main Control Room, expert analysis, behind-the-scenes insights, and the first signal from the spacecraft following separation. 
Livestream schedule (CEST): 

13:45 – Livestream begins 
16:00-16:45 – End of livestream
articles.summary: ESA and JAXA's BepiColombo mission achieves a major milestone with the successful Mercury arrival sequence. The livestream replay documents this historic moment in planetary exploration.

articles.title: Hubble tracks new decagon encircling Saturn’s south pole
articles.description: Recent observations with the NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope have revealed a giant, evolving 10-sided atmospheric wave encircling Saturn’s south pole. This discovery marks the first time a large regular-sided jet pattern has been observed in the planet’s southern hemisphere. The feature appears remarkably similar to Saturn’s famous hexagon at its northern pole, but is also distinctly different, suggesting scientists may be witnessing a new atmospheric phenomenon develop on the iconic gas giant.
articles.summary: Hubble observations reveal a giant 10-sided atmospheric wave circling Saturn's south pole, marking an extraordinary discovery in planetary meteorology. This unusual geometric pattern demonstrates the dynamic and complex atmospheres of gas giants.

articles.title: JUICE Mission to Swing by Earth on September 28
articles.description: The European Space Agency’s Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer (Juice) will return to Earth on 28 September, with flight controllers guiding the spacecraft close to our home planet to alter its speed and direction en route to Jupiter.
articles.summary: The JUICE spacecraft will perform an Earth gravity assist on September 28, maintaining its trajectory toward Jupiter's icy moons. This maneuver is essential for the European Space Agency's mission to investigate potential habitable worlds.

articles.title: How Diffractive Solar Sails Could Stop a Killer Asteroid at 100 km/s
articles.description: Asteroids don’t come with a warning label that they might one day hit Earth. While we don’t know of any currently on course to do so, we are finding thousands of new ones each year, and there’s always a potential that one could. We proved a viable technique for dealing with that eventuality - the DART mission successfully moved a small asteroid using a “kinetic impactor” - basically a big rod designed to push the asteroid off its trajectory. But DART had one big flaw - it was traveling in the same direction as the asteroid, and approached it from behind, eventually hitting it with an impactor launched while in orbit around it. That technique might work if we have enough warning, but would require years of orbital mechanical maneuvering to pull off. An alternative, proposed by researchers at Beihang University, is to use a new type of solar sail to deflect a potentially hazardous asteroid by hitting it head on.
articles.summary: Diffractive solar sails could theoretically deflect hazardous asteroids at extreme velocities, representing a revolutionary planetary defense technology. This innovative approach demonstrates humanity's growing capability to protect Earth from cosmic threats.

articles.title: First Diagnostic X-Rays in Space Mark New Era for Astronaut Health
articles.description: A team of researchers acquired the first diagnostic X-ray images during a commercial spaceflight, demonstrating that X-ray medicine can be performed in space.
articles.summary: Researchers successfully conducted the first diagnostic X-ray imaging during commercial spaceflight, opening new possibilities for astronaut health monitoring in space. This breakthrough demonstrates how space-based medical technology can advance human spaceflight safety.

articles.title: Space Rocks Carry Hundreds of Thousands of Complex Organic Molecules—and We Just Photographed Them
articles.description: Scientists have known for a while that meteorites contain the “building blocks” of life - complex organic molecules such as amino acids, simple sugars, or even the chemical rungs of DNA. But anyone who has taken an organic chemistry class knows there are plenty of other carbon-based molecules out there, and a new study from Joseph W. Frye-Jones of the National High Magnetic Field Laboratory and Florida State, which was published in The Planetary Science Journal, found tens of thousands of types of previously unseen organic compounds in two of the world’s most famous meteorites.
articles.summary: Scientists have photographed complex organic molecules in meteorites, revealing the chemical building blocks of life present in space rocks. This discovery deepens our understanding of how life's precursors exist throughout the cosmos.

articles.title: Astrophysicists use wave simulations to open a new window on dark matter
articles.description: Astrophysicists from The University of Hong Kong (HKU), working with a research team led by Beijing Normal University (BNU), have developed a more physically realistic approach to testing how ultralight, or "fuzzy," dark matter could influence gravitationally lensed images. The study is the first to make gravitational-lensing predictions directly from three-dimensional wave simulations of fuzzy dark matter.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: Astrophysicists have developed wave simulations to create a new observational window for studying dark matter. This innovative approach opens fresh avenues for understanding one of the universe's greatest mysteries.

articles.title: Bennu asteroid samples point to a surprising origin involving Jupiter
articles.description: The asteroid Bennu orbits the sun once every 1.2 years and approaches Earth every six years, passing within around 300,000 kilometers. NASA took advantage of this to collect material from the celestial body. In a spectacular operation in 2023, the US space agency collected samples from the surface of the asteroid Bennu by its OSIRIS-REx probe.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: Analysis of asteroid Bennu samples reveals surprising evidence connecting the asteroid's origin to Jupiter's gravitational influence. This discovery reshapes our understanding of how asteroids migrate through the solar system.

articles.title: Roaming black holes may tell the hidden history of galaxies
articles.description: If you want to understand the origins of black holes, Yale astronomers say, you need to look beyond the centers of galaxies and start searching in the nooks and crannies. That's where you'll find the "wanderers"—black holes whose journeys may tell the story of how the first black holes formed.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: Yale astronomers propose studying roaming black holes beyond galactic centers to understand black hole origins and galactic history. This novel approach promises new insights into black hole formation.

articles.title: The Solar System chose fire over ice from the very beginning
articles.description: Ancient iron meteorites reveal that some of the Solar System’s first solid bodies were built mostly from tiny heat-forged rock beads called chondrules, while water-rich dust was largely excluded. The finding pushes this selective planet-building process back to within the Solar System’s first million years.
articles.summary: Ancient iron meteorites reveal that the solar system's first solid bodies formed from heat-forged materials rather than icy precursors. This discovery fundamentally changes our understanding of planetary formation.

articles.title: Black holes of every size follow the same surprising rule
articles.description: Scientists have found evidence that black holes of vastly different sizes may launch powerful jets according to the same universal rule. Supermassive black holes can produce jets soon after tearing apart a star, then fire up again hundreds or thousands of days later when their feeding rate drops to about 2% of the Eddington limit. That same threshold is known to trigger jets from much smaller black holes in the Milky Way.
articles.summary: Scientists discovered that black holes of vastly different sizes follow the same surprising rule when launching powerful jets. This universal principle unifies our understanding of black hole physics.

articles.title: Scientists are about to test Einstein’s gravity with exotic matter
articles.description: Scientists have found a new way to create a controlled beam of muonium, an exotic atom containing a heavier cousin of the electron. The advance could allow researchers to test for the first time whether gravity acts on second-generation particles exactly as Einstein’s theory predicts. Any unexpected difference would be a major surprise and could potentially point toward new physics, including a hypothetical fifth force.
articles.summary: Scientists have developed a new method to create controlled beams of muonium, an exotic atom, to test Einstein's theories of gravity in unprecedented ways. This breakthrough opens new experimental pathways for fundamental physics research.

articles.title: Meet Julian Shapiro, the New York student who found 3 unusual dwarf galaxies and won $25,000
articles.description: Eighteen-year-old Julian Shapiro discovered three isolated dwarf galaxies that lack ongoing star formation, a puzzling combination for astronomers. His research suggests they could be “backsplash” galaxies that once passed near a massive galaxy, lost star-for…
articles.summary: Eighteen-year-old Julian Shapiro discovered three isolated dwarf galaxies lacking active star formation, winning $25,000 for this remarkable contribution to galactic science. His discovery adds to our understanding of rare and unusual galaxy types in the universe.

articles.title: What Is Humanity’s Place in the Cosmos?
articles.description: A lifelong fascination with terra incognita led the astrophysicist Priyamvada Natarajan to map out the universe’s most enigmatic phenomena.
articles.summary: Astrophysicist Priyamvada Natarajan shares her lifelong quest to map the universe's most extreme environments and understand humanity's place in the cosmos. Her work reveals how fascination with the unknown drives transformative scientific discovery.

articles.title: Black Holes or Black Hole Stars? Astronomers Spar Over Webb Telescope’s ‘Little Red Dots.’
articles.description: The James Webb Space Telescope spots mysterious “little red dots” everywhere. A bold new theory suggests they’re suns dozens of times larger than our entire solar system. The post Black Holes or Black Hole Stars? Astronomers Spar Over Webb Telescope’s ‘Little…
articles.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope has detected mysterious 'little red dots' throughout the universe, sparking debate about whether they are black holes or a new type of stellar object. This discovery challenges existing theories and opens new questions about cosmic structure.

articles.title: A Cosmic Catastrophe May Have Turned Neptune’s Ancient Moons Inside Out
articles.description: This image of the Neptune system, captured by the Near-Infrared Camera (NIRCam) on NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope in 2022, reveals stunning views of the planet’s rings—which have not been seen with this clarity in more than three decades—along with the pla…
articles.summary: New research suggests that a cosmic catastrophe may have dramatically altered Neptune's ancient moons, potentially turning them inside out. This James Webb Space Telescope observation reveals the dynamic and violent history of our outer solar system.

articles.title: NASA makes big step for next Artemis mission and goal of landing on the moon by 2028
articles.description: NASA is making progress towards its mission to land astronauts on the moon.
articles.summary: NASA advances its Artemis program with significant progress toward landing astronauts on the moon by 2028, marking a major milestone in lunar exploration.

articles.description: A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket launched tFalcon 9 launched 27 Starlink satellites from Space Launch Complex 4 East (SLC-4E) at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California at 9:47 p.m. EDT (6:47 p.m. local time; 0147 GMT on Sept. 20). It was a record 40th flight for o…
articles.summary: SpaceX successfully launches and deploys 27 Starlink satellites while executing a precision landing, advancing global broadband connectivity from space.

articles.title: A galaxy spinning out of sync
articles.description:
Image:
			
Though the spiral galaxy in this new image by the NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope seems serene, it hides a chaotic secret. This galaxy is NGC 4698, and it lies about 55 million light-years away in the constellation Virgo. It’s one of over one thousand galaxies in the Virgo Cluster, the nearest large cluster of galaxies bound together by gravity.
As a spiral galaxy similar to our own Milky Way galaxy, NGC 4698 has spiral arms that curl around within a thin disc of stars, gas and dust. Its centre is dominated by a galactic bulge.
The diffuse off-white glow of the galaxy’s bulge comes from stars smaller, older, and cooler than the massive blue stars that dot the galaxy’s outer disc. These tightly packed stars orbit a supermassive black hole containing millions of times the Sun’s mass. Scientists have found signs that this black hole is actively growing, drawing gas inward with its gravitational pull.
With a flat, starry disc and diffusely glowing centre, NGC 4698 looks a lot like a typical spiral galaxy — but this galaxy is far from normal. NGC 4698 is one of only a few known spiral galaxies with a bulge that extends out from the disc at a right angle. The elongation is faintly visible in this Hubble image, which shows the ghostly glow of the starry bulge peeking above and below the dusty disc. What’s more, the stars and gas nearest the galaxy’s centre rotate perpendicular to the rest of the disc.
What could cause a galaxy to be so out of sync? Astronomers have found that the culprit likely lies outside the galaxy. If NGC 4698 funneled in gas from an outside source, the newly collected gas could have formed a disc of gas and stars in the galaxy’s centre, at an angle relative to the rest of the disc. Some observations suggest that this galaxy once experienced a minor galactic merger, as evidenced by a short ‘tail’ of hydrogen streaming from one side of the galaxy.
The data used to create this image come from an observing programme (#18103; PI: Thilker) focusing on galaxies in the Virgo Cluster.
[Image Description: A spiral galaxy viewed at an angle, with a bright central bulge and winding spiral arms. The arms form a ring around the galaxy, without appearing to reach its centre. Prominent red-brown dust lanes weave through the arms, which are also dotted with bright blue and reddish regions of star formation. The galaxy is set against a dark background scattered with stars and faint distant galaxies.]
Release on esawebb.org
articles.summary: The Hubble Space Telescope captured a striking image of a spiral galaxy with unusual rotational dynamics. The observation reveals fascinating complexity in how galactic structures evolve and interact.

articles.title: Purple swirls on the Red Planet
articles.description: This image shows a prominent ice cliff near Mars’s south pole. With striking swirls of purple, pink and red, it’s a far cry from the colour palette we usually associate with the Red Planet.
articles.summary: A stunning image showcases an ice cliff near Mars's south pole, displaying vibrant purple, pink, and red hues. This breathtaking Martian landscape reveals the diverse and colorful geology of the Red Planet.

articles.title: Hubble's superbubble scene
articles.description:
Image:
			
This sprawling cosmic vista and subject of today’s ESA/Hubble Picture of the Month comes from the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC). The LMC is the largest of the small galaxies that orbit our Milky Way galaxy. At just 160 000 light-years away, the LMC offers a close look at highly active stellar birthsites like the nebula shown here. This nebula is named LHA 120-N44, or N44 for short, and it’s located in the constellation Dorado.
The appearance of this photogenic nebula is dominated by two features: a vast central void and a shell of dense, dusty gas. The central void is a ‘superbubble’ spanning roughly 210 by 140 light-years. The glittering stars at the centre of the void are responsible for its creation; through their powerful stellar winds and explosive supernovae, these stars have expelled much of the gas from which they were born.
When the stars of N44’s central star cluster swept away this gas, the expelled gas formed a shell around the superbubble. New stars are forming in this compressed gas shell, making N44 an interesting target for researchers studying the process of star formation. In particular, astronomers have turned to this nebula as an ideal place to time this process from start to finish. Their goal is to understand how long it takes from the collapse of cold gas clouds into dense knots to the moment nuclear fusion ignites in the heart of a newborn star.
Researchers used Hubble to survey N44 and take a census of its stars, cataloguing nearly half a million stars within the cluster as well as interlopers drifting in front of it. Of the stars surveyed, nearly 30 000 are what astronomers call pre-main-sequence stars, which have yet to begin fusing hydrogen into helium in their cores. This treasure trove of baby stars was discoverable thanks to the high sensitivity and fine spatial resolution of Hubble’s instruments that can pick out faint objects in crowded clusters.
The gas shell surrounding the superbubble is energised by ultraviolet radiation from massive stars, causing it to glow and highlighting several distinct features. Each feature within the broader N44 star-forming complex was catalogued by astronomer Karl Henize in the 1950s. One feature is a smaller bubble, catalogued as N44F, that is located near the upper-right corner of this image. N44F is an interstellar bubble blown by the intense stellar winds of a single hot and massive star. As this previously released Hubble closeup shows, the star’s furious winds and radiation have sculpted the surrounding bubble and created pillars of dusty gas.
The data used to create this image come from an observing programme (#14689; PI: Gouliermis) that aimed to probe stars in the N44 complex that have not yet begun fusing hydrogen into heavier elements in their cores. These data help to determine how long the process of star formation takes, as well as what masses newborn stars typically have. Hubble's sensitive observations of the lowest-mass stars in this region open a new window onto star formation in regions that, like the LMC or the galaxies of the early Universe, are poor in elements heavier than helium.
[Image Description: A dense field of stars fills the image, surrounded by wispy clouds of gas and dust. Pale blue and grey nebulosity forms an intricate web across the scene, with darker clouds of dust concentrated towards the lower right. Numerous bright stars appear in shades of blue, white and orange.]
articles.summary: Hubble captured a magnificent cosmic vista of a superbubble in the Large Magellanic Cloud, showcasing stellar nurseries and dynamic energy release. This image reveals the dramatic processes shaping galaxies.

articles.title: Following Neptune Through Opposition 2026
articles.description: Never seen Neptune for yourself? Late September 2026 presents an ideal opportunity to cross the outermost ice giant off of your ‘life list,’ as the planet reaches opposition for 2026, rising opposite to the setting Sun and riding high to the south towards local midnight.
articles.summary: Late September 2026 offers an ideal viewing opportunity to observe Neptune at opposition, making it an excellent time for amateur astronomers to observe the distant ice giant. This celestial event showcases the beauty and accessibility of our outer solar system.
